Number Series.title: Number Series
Number Series.weight: About 18 to 22 of the 52 Quantitative Skills questions — the largest type
Number Series.oneLine: A short run of numbers, letters or both follows a hidden rule, and you supply the term that is missing.

blocks.text: Series questions are the largest single block on the Quantitative Skills section. You are shown four to seven terms that follow a rule nobody tells you, and you supply a term that is missing. The terms may be whole numbers, fractions, decimals, letters, Roman numerals or a mix of these.

The rules are not clever. Almost every series on this test is built from adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing or stepping through the alphabet. What makes the questions hard is the clock. The section gives you 52 questions in 30 minutes, which is about 35 seconds each, and no calculator. Speed here comes from running the same procedure every time, not from being quick at arithmetic.
The method

items: Read the whole series before you write anything. Notice what kind of terms these are, and notice exactly where the blank sits.
Write the difference between each pair of neighboring terms in the gap between them. Do this even when you think you already see the pattern.
If the differences are all the same, the rule is add that number. You are done.
If the differences are not the same, take the differences of the differences. If those are constant, the series is progressive and the next gap is predictable.
If the terms climb or fall steeply, look for a ratio instead. Divide each term by the one before it.
If none of that works, stop treating the series as one chain. Read every other term. Two simple series braided together look like one complicated series.
Apply your rule to get the term the item asks for, then test the rule against a pair you have not used yet. A rule that explains only the front of the series is the wrong rule.

blocks.text: Before you answer, count which position the blank occupies. Items that put the blank in the middle, or at the very start, are the ones students miss — not because the rule is hard but because they compute the term after the blank instead of the blank itself. Once you have a candidate, drop it back into the series and read the whole thing forward.
Take the differences first
Take $7, 12, 17, 22, 27$. Under the gaps write $5, 5, 5, 5$. Constant, so add five and the next term is $32$. That is most series questions, and it takes about eight seconds.

Now take $5, 6, 9, 14, 21, 30$. The differences are $1, 3, 5, 7, 9$, which are not constant — but the differences of those are $2, 2, 2, 2$. The gap grows by two every step, so the next gap is $11$ and the next term is $41$. A series whose gaps grow by a fixed amount is called progressive, and taking a second round of differences is the only thing you need to crack it.

When a series climbs steeply the differences will never settle, so divide instead of subtracting. In $3, 12, 48, 192$ each term is four times the one before it, and the next term is $768$. Falling series work the same way. In $405, 135, 45, 15$ each term is one third of the last, so the next is $5$.
The families you will meet

Every series on the test is one of these shapes. Read the table once, then work through the examples below — recognizing the family is most of the battle, because once you name it the arithmetic is trivial.

head: Family
A series of this kind
The rule
Next term
rows: odd places add $4$; even places subtract $5$
first letter ahead two, second back one
move ahead three letters, keep the pair
Fractions, top adds and bottom doubles
inside a block add $2$; each block starts $5$ higher
each number is followed by its square

blocks.text: Letter series

Letters are numbers in disguise. A is 1 and Z is 26. Write the position numbers under the letters and a letter series becomes a number series, which you already know how to solve. You do not need to recite the whole alphabet with its numbers; you need six anchors. A is 1, F is 6, K is 11, P is 16, U is 21, Z is 26. From an anchor you can count forward two or three letters faster than you can count from the beginning.

Two things to watch. First, a letter series can run past Z and wrap round to A, so treat the alphabet as a loop rather than a line. Second, when the terms are pairs or triples of letters, each position usually follows its own rule. Read all the first letters together, then all the second letters together, and do not try to see both at once.
When the repetition is the pattern

Some letter series carry their rule in how many times a letter is written rather than in which letter it is. In Q, RR, SSS, TTTT the letter advances by one and the number of copies advances by one, so the next term is UUUUU. Count the copies before you look at anything else; if the counts are $1, 2, 3, 4$ you have found the rule and the letters will follow an easy pattern of their own.

Mixed strings work the same way. In B4, D8, F12, H16 the letters and the numbers are two separate series that happen to be printed next to each other. Solve them separately — letters ahead two, numbers up four — and put the answers back together as J20. The same applies when Roman numerals are mixed with Arabic ones: convert every Roman numeral to a plain number first, and the series usually turns out to be something ordinary like counting by two.
Where the blank sits

Four formats appear, and they are not equally easy. You may be asked for the next term, for the next two terms, for a blank in the middle of the series, or for the missing first term. The last two are where students lose points. With a medial blank, find the rule from the terms on both sides of the gap and then check that your answer works forwards and backwards. With an initial blank, you have to run the rule in reverse: if the series adds five going right, it subtracts five going left.
Numbers worth having ready

blocks.stem: Look at this series: 9, 16, 23, ___, 37, 44. What number should fill the blank?
blocks.walkthrough: Take the differences you can see: $16-9=7$ and $23-16=7$, and at the other end $44-37=7$. The series adds seven. The blank is the fourth term, so it is $23+7=30$, and the check works both ways because $30+7=37$. The wrong choices are all near misses — they come from settling on a difference of five or six after glancing at only one pair, which is why you take at least two differences before committing.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: 4, 30, 8, 26, 12, 22, 16, ___. What number comes next?
blocks.walkthrough: The differences swing wildly — $+26$, $-22$, $+18$ — which is the signal to stop reading it as one chain. Read the odd positions: 4, 8, 12, 16, going up by four. Read the even positions: 30, 26, 22, going down by four. The blank is the eighth term, an even position, so it continues 30, 26, 22 and the answer is 18. The trap is 20, which is what you get by carrying the odd chain forward from 16 without noticing which position you are filling.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: ___, PR, SU, VX, YA. What letter pair belongs in the blank at the beginning?
blocks.walkthrough: Treat the two positions separately. The first letters are P, S, V, Y — that is 16, 19, 22, 25, going up by three — so the missing first letter is $16-3=13$, which is M. The second letters are R, U, X, A — 18, 21, 24, then a wrap round to 1 — also up by three, so the missing second letter is $18-3=15$, which is O. The answer is MO. LN steps back four instead of three; NP steps back only two; MP gets the first letter right and then reuses the wrong gap inside the pair.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: 2, 8, 5, 20, 17, 68, ___. What number comes next?
blocks.walkthrough: The terms rise, fall, rise, fall, so two operations are alternating. Check them in order: $2\times4=8$, $8-3=5$, $5\times4=20$, $20-3=17$, $17\times4=68$. The pattern is multiply by four, subtract three, repeating, and the step after $\times 4$ is $-3$, so the answer is $68-3=65$. The trap is 272, which applies the operation you just used instead of the one that comes next; 71 reverses the sign of the subtraction.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: C3, F9, I27, L81, ___. What comes next?
blocks.walkthrough: Split the letters from the numbers. C, F, I, L are 3, 6, 9, 12, so the next letter is 15, which is O. The numbers 3, 9, 27, 81 have no constant difference but a constant ratio of three, so the next is $81\times3=243$. Put them back together for O243. M243 advances the letter by one, P243 advances it by four and O162 doubles the number instead of tripling it — each wrong choice gets one of the two series right and the other wrong, which is exactly how these distractors are built.

blocks.text: The traps

items: A rule that fits only the front of the series. Two terms will agree with almost any rule. Test yours on the last pair as well as the first.
Answering with the term after the blank. On medial-blank and initial-blank items this is the most common single error, and the test always offers that term as a choice.
Reducing a fraction. In $\frac{1}{2}, \frac{2}{4}, \frac{3}{8}, \frac{4}{16}$ the pattern lives in the unreduced numbers. Simplify $\frac{2}{4}$ to $\frac{1}{2}$ and the pattern vanishes.
Reading an interleaved series as one chain. If the differences alternate between large positive and large negative, you are looking at two series, not one.
Miscounting the alphabet. Under time pressure it is easy to slide one letter. Count from the nearest anchor, not from A.
Choices one step short or one step long. When a series is $+6$ each time, the choices will include the term before and the term after the one you want. Recount the position.

blocks.text: When you are stuck

items: Give it 15 seconds of differences and ratios. If neither settles, check the odd and even positions. If that fails too, guess and move on — a series you cannot see in 30 seconds is not worth 90.
Work backward from the choices. Drop each option into the blank and read the series aloud in your head; the right one makes the whole line regular, and usually only one does.
Eliminate by size. If the series is climbing, any choice smaller than the term before the blank is out. If it is falling, any choice larger is out. That often leaves two.
Never leave a series blank. There is no penalty for a wrong answer on the HSPT, so an unanswered question is strictly worse than a guess.

blocks.text: Worth memorizing

items: The alphabet anchors: A is 1, F is 6, K is 11, P is 16, U is 21, Z is 26.
The squares up to $15^2=225$ and the cubes up to $10^3=1000$.
The procedure itself. Differences, then differences of differences, then ratios, then odd and even positions. Running it in that order without thinking is what buys you the time.

Comparisons.title: Comparisons
Comparisons.weight: About 16 to 19 of the 52 questions, split between figure comparisons and expression comparisons
Comparisons.oneLine: Three labeled quantities or figures are given, and you choose the statement that correctly orders them.

blocks.text: A comparison item hands you three things labeled A, B and C and asks for the best answer. The four choices are not numbers — they are statements about how the three compare, built from $=$, $\lt$ and $\gt$. Your job is to work out what A, B and C actually are and then find the statement that is true of them.

Two different kinds of item share this format, and they need different work. Sometimes A, B and C are number or algebra expressions, and you work each one out. Sometimes they are figures — whole shapes, or parts of one shape. Then the choices compare lengths, angles, areas, shaded parts or the number of sides and corners. Both appear on every form of the test.

Evaluate all three quantities before you read the choices, and write the three values down. Reading the choices first is the biggest time sink on this question type: you end up checking four statements against numbers you have not worked out yet, which means computing the same thing three or four times over. Three values first, then one pass through the choices.
Type one: comparing expressions

items: Work out A completely. Write the number down next to the letter.
Do the same for B, then for C. Do not skip one because it looks obviously biggest.
Put all three in the same form before you compare. All decimals, or all fractions over the same denominator — never a mixture.
Now read the choices, one at a time, and test each against your three numbers.
If a choice makes two claims joined by and, check both halves. The choice is wrong if either half is wrong.

blocks.text: Putting everything in one form is worth the two seconds it costs. $\frac{3}{8}$, $0.4$ and $35\%$ are hard to rank while they are wearing different clothes and trivial once they are $0.375$, $0.4$ and $0.35$. Decimals are usually the fastest common form, because you can compare them left to right one digit at a time.

blocks.stem: Examine A, B and C and choose the best answer.   A. $25\%$ of $88$   B. $\frac{1}{3}$ of $63$   C. $0.4 \times 55$
blocks.walkthrough: Evaluate before you read anything else. A is a quarter of 88, which is $22$. B is a third of 63, which is $21$. C is $0.4 \times 55$, which is $22$. Write down $22$, $21$, $22$ and only now look at the choices: A and C are equal and both beat B, so the last choice is the one. Notice the second choice — it is half right, because A really is greater than B, but $B = C$ is false, and a statement joined by and needs both halves to hold.

blocks.stem: Examine A, B and C and choose the best answer.   A. $3 + 4 \times 5$   B. $(3 + 4) \times 5$   C. $3 \times 4 + 5$
blocks.walkthrough: These are the same three numbers in three arrangements, so the item is really about order of operations. A multiplies first: $4 \times 5 = 20$, then $3 + 20 = 23$. B has parentheses, so $3 + 4 = 7$ first, then $7 \times 5 = 35$. C multiplies first again: $3 \times 4 = 12$, then $12 + 5 = 17$. That gives $35 \gt 23 \gt 17$, which is B, A, C. The trap is working A from left to right, getting $35$, and concluding that A and B are equal.

blocks.stem: Examine A, B and C and choose the best answer.   A. $\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^2$   B. $\sqrt{\frac{9}{16}}$   C. $\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{4}{3}$
blocks.walkthrough: A is $\frac{9}{16}$, or $0.5625$. B is the square root of $\frac{9}{16}$, which is $\frac{3}{4}$, or $0.75$. C is a number multiplied by its own reciprocal, which is always $1$. So C is largest, then B, then A. The point worth keeping is what happened to $\frac{3}{4}$: squaring made it smaller and taking the root made it larger, because it sits between zero and one. Anyone who assumes squaring always grows a number picks the first choice.

blocks.text: Type two: comparing figures

Figures on the HSPT are not necessarily drawn to scale. A line that looks longer may not be. An angle that looks square may be $80^\circ$. Two shaded regions that look equal may not be. Reason only from what the figure states — labeled measurements, tick marks, right-angle boxes, the words square or equilateral — and never from what the picture looks like.

That rule is the whole question type. The figures are drawn imprecisely on purpose, because the item is testing whether you know that a square's diagonal is longer than its side, not whether you can eyeball a drawing. If a statement cannot be settled from the stated properties, it is not the answer, however true it looks.

items: List what you are actually told. Side lengths, angle measures, the name of the shape, any marks showing that parts are equal.
Derive what follows. If two angles of a triangle are given, the third is $180^\circ$ minus their sum. If a square's perimeter is given, its side is a quarter of it.
Write the derived numbers down. Do not carry them in your head while reading four statements.
Test each choice against those numbers, and reject any choice that depends on how the drawing looks.
If a figure is missing a measurement you would need, the honest answer may be that the two cannot be compared. Check whether a choice says so.

blocks.text: Because this page cannot show you a drawing, the two examples below describe the figures in words. That is useful practice in itself: the first thing to do with a figure on the test is translate it into a short list of stated facts, which is exactly what these stems already are.

blocks.stem: In triangle $DEF$, angle $D$ measures $40^\circ$ and angle $E$ measures $95^\circ$. Choose the best answer.
options: $\angle F$ is the largest angle in the triangle.
$\angle D + \angle F$ is greater than $\angle E$.
$\angle D$, $\angle E$ and $\angle F$ are all equal.
blocks.walkthrough: Derive the missing angle first: the three angles of any triangle add to $180^\circ$, so $\angle F = 180 - 40 - 95 = 45^\circ$. Now your three numbers are $40$, $95$ and $45$. The third choice is true, since $45 \gt 40$. The first is false because $\angle E$ is the largest. The second misses by ten degrees — $40 + 45 = 85$, which is less than $95$ — and it is the choice most students accept without computing, because two angles sounds like more than one.

blocks.stem: Square $A$ has a perimeter of $24$ cm. Rectangle $B$ is $8$ cm long and $4$ cm wide. Circle $C$ has a radius of $4$ cm. Choose the best answer.
options: The area of $A$ is less than the area of $B$.
$A$ and $B$ have equal perimeters, but $A$ has the greater area.
$A$, $B$ and $C$ all have the same area.
blocks.walkthrough: Turn every figure into numbers before comparing anything. Square A has side $24 \div 4 = 6$, so its area is $36$ and its perimeter is $24$. Rectangle B has area $8 \times 4 = 32$ and perimeter $2(8) + 2(4) = 24$. Circle C has area $\pi \times 4^2 = 16\pi$, which is about $50.3$. Both halves of the second choice hold: the perimeters match at $24$, and $36 \gt 32$. The third choice is the trap for anyone weighing a radius of $4$ against a side of $6$ by eye — the circle is in fact the largest of the three in area.

blocks.text: The facts these questions lean on

head: Situation
What is true
rows: $x^3 \lt x^2 \lt x \lt \sqrt{x}$. Squaring shrinks it; taking a root grows it.
Area $s^2$; perimeter $4s$; the diagonal is longer than a side.
Area $\frac{1}{2}bh$; the three angles add to $180^\circ$; the longest side lies opposite the largest angle.
Six faces, 12 edges, eight vertices; volume $s^3$; surface area $6s^2$.
Do not mean equal areas. Of all rectangles with a given perimeter, the square encloses the most area.
Doubles the perimeter but multiplies the area by four.

blocks.text: The traps

items: A statement that is true but is not the best answer. The instruction says best for a reason. When two choices both look right, one of them is usually true of only part of the figure, or true only if the drawing is accurate. Prefer the one that follows from the stated facts alone.
A compound choice where only one half holds. Anything joined by and contains two claims and both must be true. Check the half you are less sure of first.
Judging shaded area by eye. If a choice compares shaded regions, count the equal parts the figure is divided into. If nothing tells you the parts are equal, you cannot compare them.

Forgetting what squaring does below one. $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}$, which is smaller. This is the most reliable trap in the section, and it covers $0.3^2 = 0.09$ and $0.9^2 = 0.81$ as well.
Comparing unlike measurements. If one quantity is a perimeter and another is an area, ranking them means nothing. Read what each letter measures before you order them.
Assuming a right angle. Unless the little square is drawn or the problem says so, an angle that looks like $90^\circ$ is just an angle.

blocks.text: When you are stuck

items: Estimate. You rarely need exact values to rank three quantities. $\frac{7}{15}$ is a shade under a half, and $48\%$ of $610$ is close to $300$. Ranking is easier than computing.
Eliminate on one letter. If you are certain A is the largest, cross out every choice that puts anything above A. Two choices usually go at once.
Look for the equals sign. Test writers like items in which two of the three come out the same. If a quick look suggests two of your values match, check the choice containing $=$ first.

Guess and move on. There is no penalty for a wrong answer on the HSPT, so mark your best remaining choice and go. A comparison you have half-solved still gives you a one-in-two guess, which is a fine trade for 30 seconds.

blocks.text: Worth memorizing

items: The fraction, decimal and percent table above. Knowing $\frac{3}{8} = 0.375$ on sight saves you the long division every time.
Area and perimeter for the square, rectangle, triangle and circle.
A cube has six faces, 12 edges and eight vertices.
Between zero and one, squaring makes a number smaller and a square root makes it bigger. Above one, the reverse.
Evaluate first, read the choices second. That is a habit rather than a fact, and it is worth more than any of the formulas.

Number Manipulation.title: Number Manipulation
Number Manipulation.oneLine: A single arithmetic relationship is stated entirely in words, and you translate it into an equation and solve for the unknown.

blocks.text: These items give you one sentence. No diagram, no story about trains, no list of quantities to rank — just a relationship between numbers, written out in English, with one number left unnamed. What number is four more than three times seven? The arithmetic is easy. Turning the sentence into an equation is the whole test.

That is worth saying plainly, because it changes how you practice. If you get one of these wrong, it is almost never because you cannot multiply. It is because you wrote $5 - n$ where the sentence said $n - 5$, or because you took the square of a sum when the sentence asked for the sum of the squares. Translation is a skill, and it can be drilled.
The method

items: Read the whole sentence to the end before you write anything. These sentences often reverse themselves halfway through.
Name the unknown. Write let $n$ be the number at the top of your scratch space, and be clear about which number $n$ is — the one the question asks for, not the one it mentions first.
Translate phrase by phrase, in the order the words arrive, using the table below. Write the equation on paper. Do not hold it in your head.
Stop and check operand order on every subtraction and every division. This is where the points are lost.
Solve. Undo the operations in reverse order: whatever was done last, undo first.
Reread the question and answer what it actually asked. If it asked for twice the number, do not stop at the number.

blocks.text: Order matters on subtraction and division. Five less than a number is $n - 5$. Five less a number is $5 - n$. The same flip runs through six subtracted from a number, which is $n - 6$, and a number subtracted from six, which is $6 - n$. Test writers place both the correct answer and the reversed answer among the choices every single time, so a reversal never looks like a mistake — it looks like an option.
Translation table

head: What the words say
What you write
rows: of (after a fraction or a percent)
the quotient of $a$ and $b$; $a$ divided by $b$

blocks.text: Two rows in that table deserve a second look. Divided into reverses the order you expect: four divided into 20 is $20 \div 4 = 5$, not $4 \div 20$. And the difference between is written large number first, because a difference on this test is not meant to come out negative.
Percents and fractions of a quantity

The word of after a fraction or a percent always means multiply. Two thirds of 51 is $51 \div 3 \times 2 = 34$. Thirty percent of 90 is $0.30 \times 90 = 27$. With no calculator, the fast route is to break the percent into pieces you can do in your head rather than to multiply decimals.

head: Percent
Fast way to get it
rows: take $10\%$, then add half of that
divide by 4, or halve it twice
halve it, then add half of that again

blocks.text: So $15\%$ of 80 is $8 + 4 = 12$, and $75\%$ of 48 is $24 + 12 = 36$. Both take about three seconds and neither needs a written multiplication.
Squares, cubes and roots inside a sentence

When powers appear in words, translate them one phrase at a time and then combine. The cube of three is $27$ and the square of four is $16$, so the cube of three is $11$ more than the square of four. The square root of 81 added to the square of five is $9 + 25 = 34$.

Watch the two phrasings that sound alike and are not. The square of the sum of two and five means add first: $(2 + 5)^2 = 49$. The sum of the squares of two and five means square first: $4 + 25 = 29$. Whichever operation is named last in the phrase is the one you perform last.
Working backward
Working backward means two different useful things on this question type, and both are worth having.

The first is undoing a chain of operations. A number is multiplied by three, then seven is subtracted and the result is 26. Rather than build an equation, run the sentence in reverse and invert each step: add seven to $26$ to get $33$, then divide by three to get $11$. Check it forward — $11 \times 3 = 33$ and $33 - 7 = 26$ — and you are done in less time than writing $3n - 7 = 26$ would take.

The second is testing the answer choices. When the translation is awkward, stop translating and start substituting. You have four candidates and a sentence you can check a candidate against, and checking is much faster than solving. Start with the second-smallest choice: if it comes out too small you know to go up, and you have often cut the work in half on the first try.
Estimating to eliminate

With 35 seconds a question you do not always need the exact value. If a question asks for $48\%$ of $610$, it is a shade under half of $600$, so anything far from $300$ is gone. If it asks for the square of a number between $7$ and $8$, the answer lies between $49$ and $64$. Rough size is often enough to leave one choice standing, and one choice standing is an answer.

blocks.stem: What number is four more than three times seven?
blocks.walkthrough: Translate in the order the words come. Three times seven is $3 \times 7 = 21$, and four more than that is $21 + 4 = 25$. The choice 33 is what you get from $3 \times (7 + 4)$, adding before multiplying; 31 comes from $7 \times 4 + 3$, which uses the same three numbers in the wrong roles; 21 is the value you stop at if you forget the last three words. Finishing the sentence is half the work.

blocks.stem: What number is one half of $\frac{3}{5}$ of 60?
blocks.walkthrough: Work from the inside out. $\frac{3}{5}$ of 60 is $60 \div 5 \times 3 = 36$, and one half of $36$ is $18$. The trap is 36, which is where you land if you translate the first of and forget the second. You can also do it in one move: half of $\frac{3}{5}$ is $\frac{3}{10}$, and $\frac{3}{10}$ of 60 is $18$, which is the faster route once you trust it.

blocks.stem: Twenty percent of what number is six more than 10?
blocks.walkthrough: Deal with the right-hand side first, because it is closed: six more than 10 is $16$. Now the sentence reads twenty percent of what number is 16, so $0.20n = 16$ and $n = 16 \div 0.20 = 80$. Check it: $20\%$ of 80 is $16$. The trap is 320, from multiplying $16 \times 20$ instead of dividing by $0.20$ — whenever a percent under 100 is taken of the unknown, the unknown must be larger than the result, so 32 and 48 are also too small to survive a size check.

blocks.stem: The number nine is seven less than half of what number?
blocks.walkthrough: Seven less than half of a number is $\frac{n}{2} - 7$, not $7 - \frac{n}{2}$, so the equation is $\frac{n}{2} - 7 = 9$. Add seven to both sides for $\frac{n}{2} = 16$, then double for $n = 32$. Read it back: half of 32 is 16, and seven less than 16 is nine. The choice 4 is the reversal, from $\frac{n}{2} = 9 - 7$; 16 is stopping at the half instead of the whole; 23 comes from adding $7 \times 2$ to nine.

blocks.stem: The square of what number is eight more than seven times that number?
blocks.walkthrough: The equation is $n^2 = 7n + 8$, which is not something you want to rearrange under time pressure — so test the choices instead. For 4: $16$ against $28 + 8 = 36$, too small. For 6: $36$ against $42 + 8 = 50$, still too small, but closer. For 8: $64$ against $56 + 8 = 64$, a match. For 9: $81$ against $63 + 8 = 71$, now too large, which confirms that 8 is the only crossing point. Notice that the squares are catching up as the numbers grow; once you see the gap closing, you know which direction to move.

blocks.text: The traps

items: Reversed subtraction. Less than and subtracted from both put the named number second. The reversed value is always among the choices.
Reversed division. Divided into is the opposite of divided by. Read it twice.
Stopping one step early. If the sentence asks for twice a number, or for the number's square, the number itself will be sitting there as a choice.
Answering the wrong unknown. Some sentences mention two quantities. Underline the one the question is asking for before you solve.
Order of operations inside the words. Four more than three times seven multiplies first. Three times four more than seven adds first. The word order tells you which.
Percent of an unknown. If a percent below 100 is taken of the unknown and equals a result, the unknown is larger than the result. A choice smaller than the result cannot be right.
Sum of squares against square of a sum. They are different numbers and both usually appear in the choices.

blocks.text: When you are stuck

items: Substitute the choices. This is the reliable fallback on this question type, because verifying is always easier than solving. Work from the middle outward so that a miss tells you which way to go.
Estimate the size and eliminate. Decide whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than the number in the sentence, then cross out everything on the wrong side.
Break the sentence at the word is. Everything before it is one expression and everything after it is another. Translate the closed side first — it is usually a plain number.
Try small numbers if the sentence is abstract. Substituting $n = 2$ into a relationship you are unsure of will usually show you at once whether you have the order right.
Guess and move on. There is no penalty for a wrong answer on the HSPT, so every question deserves a mark, and a 30-second question is not worth two minutes.

blocks.text: Worth memorizing

items: The translation table above, especially the four rows about subtraction and the two about division.
The percent shortcuts: $10\%$, $5\%$, $25\%$ and $50\%$ can all be done by halving and shifting a decimal point.
The squares to $15^2 = 225$ and the cubes to $10^3 = 1000$. These turn up constantly in verbal statements and you should never be computing them.
Undo in reverse order. Whatever the sentence did last, you undo first.

Letter Series.title: Letter Series
Letter Series.weight: About four of the 52 Quantitative Skills questions
Letter Series.oneLine: A run of letters, or of letters and numbers together, follows a rule you have to name before you can supply the missing term.

blocks.text: Four or five of the series items on a form are built from letters rather than numbers. The terms may be single letters, pairs like GT and HS, triples like MCF, groups that repeat a letter several times, or a letter tied to a number as in B5 and D9. The task never changes: name the rule, then supply the term the item asks for.

These questions are worth practicing separately from number series because the arithmetic is trivial and the bookkeeping is not. Almost nobody misses one of these because they cannot add two. They miss it because they counted the alphabet wrong, or moved one letter of a pair and forgot the other, or wrote the right two letters in the wrong order.
The method

items: Before the section starts, write the alphabet down the margin of your scratch paper with the position number beside every letter. You write it once and use it on every letter item on the form.
Read the whole series and count how many characters each term holds. One letter, two, three, a letter and a number — that count tells you how many rules you are looking for.
Look for a character that never changes. A letter appearing in the same position in every term is scenery; copy it straight into your answer and stop thinking about it.
Take each remaining position on its own. Write the position numbers under all the first letters, then under all the second letters, and find the step for each column separately.
Write your answer out character by character, in order, from those separate rules.
Check it against the term on the other side of the blank. If the item gives a term after the gap, your answer has to lead into it as well as follow from the term before it.

blocks.text: Two rules running at once is the normal case, not the hard case. In GT, HS, IR the first letter climbs and the second falls, and the only reliable way to see that is to handle the two columns one after the other. Trying to watch both at the same time is what produces answers like KQ, where one column is right and the other never moved.
Count positions, do not recite

Reciting the alphabet under time pressure is how you slide one letter, and one letter is always among the choices. Count instead. Six anchors are enough to place any letter quickly: A is 1, F is 6, K is 11, P is 16, U is 21 and Z is 26. To find the letter five past R, start from P at 16, so R is 18, and 18 plus 5 is 23, which is W. That is faster and steadier than singing through the alphabet from the beginning.

The alphabet is a loop on this test, not a line. A series that steps forward three from X does not stop at Z; it wraps round, so X, then A, then D. When a column of letters runs into the end of the alphabet, subtract 26 and keep going: 24 plus 3 is 27, and 27 minus 26 is 1, which is A.
The shapes you will meet

Every letter item on the test is one of the shapes below. Read the table once and then work the examples, because naming the shape is most of the work. Once you know that one letter is fixed and the others advance two, the answer takes about five seconds.

blocks.text: A letter that stands still

In three-letter terms one position is often frozen. MCF, MEF, MGF holds the M and the F and moves only the middle letter. PDQ, PGT, PJW holds the P at the front and moves the other two. Find the frozen letter first, write it into the answer right away and you have turned a three-letter problem into a one-letter or two-letter problem. The choices will include a term that moves the frozen letter as well, which is why it is worth naming it out loud before you go on.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: TBW, TDW, TFW, ___, TJW. What term is missing?
blocks.walkthrough: The first letter is T in every term and the last is W in every term, so both are scenery. That leaves the middle column: B, D, F, blank, J. In position numbers that reads $2$, $4$, $6$, blank, $10$, climbing by two, so the missing letter is $8$, which is H. The answer is THW, and it checks forward because H to J is another step of two. TIW moves the middle letter only one; THX moves the last letter, which never moves; WHT is the right three letters written backward, and a reversed term is offered on nearly every item of this kind.

blocks.text: Two letters walking in opposite directions

The most common two-letter shape sends one letter up the alphabet and the other down. GT, HS, IR looks complicated until you split it: G, H, I is plus one, and T, S, R is minus one. Handle the columns in order, write the two answers down, then join them. The danger is that both columns are moving by one, so a term with the columns swapped still looks plausible at a glance.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: FU, GT, HS, IR, ___. What term comes next?
blocks.walkthrough: First column: F, G, H, I are $6, 7, 8, 9$, so the next is $10$, which is J. Second column: U, T, S, R are $21, 20, 19, 18$, so the next is $17$, which is Q. Join them for JQ. JR repeats the second letter instead of stepping it back, KQ pushes the first letter two, and QJ is your own answer written backward — the choice that catches students who solve the columns in the order they find them rather than the order they are printed.

blocks.text: When the repetition is the rule

Some series carry their pattern in how many times a letter is written. In R, QQ, P, OO, N the letters simply walk backward one at a time, and on top of that every second term is doubled. In K, L, K, LL, K, LLL, K a single K sits between groups of L that gain one letter each time, and the K is doing nothing at all except separating the groups. Count the copies before you look at the letters. If the counts run 1, 2, 3, 4 or alternate 1, 2, 1, 2, you have found half the rule already.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: S, RR, Q, PP, O, ___. What term comes next?
blocks.walkthrough: Read the letters alone: S, R, Q, P, O, which is $19, 18, 17, 16, 15$, stepping back one, so the sixth letter is $14$, which is N. Now read the counts alone: one, two, one, two, one, so the sixth term is doubled. Put the two rules together and the answer is NN. The choice N drops the doubling, NNN invents a count that never appears in the series, and MM skips a letter by counting the doubled terms as two steps instead of one.

blocks.text: A letter and a number at the same time

Mixed terms such as B5, D9, F13 or C3, F12, I48 are two separate series printed side by side. Cover the numbers with a finger and solve the letters; cover the letters and solve the numbers. The two rules do not have to be the same kind: in C3, F12, I48 the letters add three each time while the numbers multiply by four. Every wrong choice on an item like this gets one half right and the other half wrong, so both halves have to be checked.

Watch the order of the characters as well as their values. In 5J, K9, 5L, M9 the letters run J, K, L, M, N straight through and the numbers alternate 5 and 9, but the terms holding a 5 put the number first and the terms holding a 9 put it last. Getting the two characters right and printing them the wrong way round is a wrong answer, and it is always one of the four choices.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: D2, G6, J18, ___. What term comes next?
blocks.walkthrough: Split the terms. The letters D, G, J are $4, 7, 10$, climbing by three, so the next letter is $13$, which is M. The numbers 2, 6, 18 have no constant difference, but each is three times the one before it, so the next is $18 \times 3 = 54$. The answer is M54. M24 adds six to the number instead of tripling it, L54 advances the letter only two, and N54 advances it four — three choices, each of which solves exactly one of the two strands.

blocks.text: When the blank comes first

An item that asks what term should come first is the same problem run backward. Find the rule from the terms you can see, then invert it: a column that adds four going right subtracts four going left, and a column that steps back one going right steps forward one going left. Students lose these by finding the rule correctly and then applying it in the direction they read, which lands them one term past the front of the series instead of one term before it.

blocks.stem: Look at this series: ___, HL, LP, PT, TX. What term should come first?
blocks.walkthrough: Both columns move the same way here. First letters H, L, P, T are $8, 12, 16, 20$, jumping four, so the term before H is $8 - 4 = 4$, which is D. Second letters L, P, T, X are $12, 16, 20, 24$, also jumping four, so the letter before L is $12 - 4 = 8$, which is H. The answer is DH. CG steps both letters back five, DL gets the first letter right and leaves the second where it was, and HD is DH reversed.

blocks.text: The traps

items: Reciting instead of counting. Slide one letter early in the alphabet and every letter after it is wrong. Count from the nearest anchor, and write the alphabet in the margin so you never have to recite at all.
The reversed term. XM for MX, PK for KP, FIM for MIF. Your own answer written backward is offered on nearly every letter item on the test. Read your letters left to right once more before you mark.
Moving one column and forgetting the other. Two letters means two rules. A choice that gets the first letter right and leaves the second unchanged is the single most common distractor here.
Missing a letter that never moves. If the same letter sits in the same position in every term, it belongs in your answer untouched. Choices that shift it look almost right.
Reading a mixed term as one rule. In C3, F12, I48 the letters add and the numbers multiply. Solve the strands separately or you will force one rule onto both.
Following the wrong strand. In K, L, K, LL, K, LLL the K is a separator, not part of the pattern. Continuing it gives K or KKKK, and both are offered.
Stopping at Z. The alphabet wraps. If a column runs past 26, subtract 26 and carry on from A.

blocks.text: When you are stuck

items: Number the letters. Write the position of every letter under it and the series usually turns into something like $4, 7, 10$, which you can read at a glance.
Test the choices. Drop each one into the blank and read the whole series through. On letter items only one choice normally survives a reading in both directions.
Eliminate on direction. If a column is climbing, any choice that moves that letter backward is gone, and that often leaves two.
Guess and move on. There is no penalty for a wrong answer on the HSPT, so mark your best remaining choice. Four letter items are not worth four minutes.

blocks.text: Worth memorizing

items: The alphabet anchors: A is 1, F is 6, K is 11, P is 16, U is 21, Z is 26.
Z wraps round to A. Past 26, subtract 26.
Each position in a multi-character term has its own rule, and the rules can be of different kinds.
A frozen letter is scenery. Copy it and move on.
The habit that pays for itself: write the alphabet with its numbers in the margin before you answer the first question of the section.

Geometric Comparison.title: Geometric Comparison
Geometric Comparison.weight: About six of the 52 Quantitative Skills questions
Geometric Comparison.oneLine: Three labeled figures are compared on area, perimeter, angle measure or length, and you pick the two-part statement that is true of all three.

blocks.text: A geometric comparison shows you three small drawings labeled $A$, $B$ and $C$ with their measurements printed on them. The four choices are not numbers. Each one is a compound statement such as The area of $A$ equals the area of $C$, and the area of $B$ is greater than the area of $A$, and exactly one of them is true of all three figures.

Four things get compared, and the stem always says which: area, perimeter or distance around, the measure of an angle marked $x$, or the length of a labeled segment. Read that word first. A student who computes three areas for a question that asked about perimeters has done all the work and still cannot answer, and the choices are written so that the area ordering is a different ordering from the perimeter ordering.
The method

items: Read the stem and name the measure. Area, perimeter, angle or length. Write that word at the top of your scratch space.
Copy the labeled numbers off each figure. Side lengths, the two given angles, the radius — whatever is actually printed.
Compute all three values before you look at a single choice. Write $A$, $B$ and $C$ down the page with a number beside each.
Rank your three numbers and say the ordering to yourself: they are all equal, or two match and one is bigger, or they run $A$, $C$, $B$.
Now read the choices once. Each has two clauses joined by and. Test the clauses separately and reject the choice the moment either clause fails.
If two choices survive, you have made an arithmetic slip somewhere. Recompute the value that appears in both.

blocks.text: Compute all three before the choices, every time. If you read the choices first you end up computing the area of $A$ once for each choice that mentions it, which is four times the work in a section that gives you 35 seconds a question. Three numbers, then one pass down the list.
Read the labels, not the picture

The drawings are not to scale and are frequently drawn to mislead. In one item on this site figure $B$ is a rectangle 10 cm by 2 cm, easily the widest of the three on the page, and it has the smallest area of the three. In another, figure $C$ is a square 5 cm on a side that looks smaller across than a rectangle 8 cm by 3 cm, and it is the largest. Width is not area. Height is not perimeter. Nothing you can see with your eye is evidence.

The same goes the other way. If a figure is called a square, every side is equal even when the drawing looks oblong. If a triangle is called equilateral, all three sides match the one number printed on it. If a right-angle box is drawn, the angle is $90^\circ$; if no box is drawn, an angle that looks square is just an angle. Work from the words and the numbers only.
The formulas you need
The whole question type runs on six formulas and four angle totals. There is nothing else to learn, so learn these to the point where you are not deriving them under time pressure.

head: Figure
Area
Distance around
rows: split it into rectangles and add

blocks.stem: Figure $A$ is a rectangle 6 cm by 4 cm, figure $B$ is a rectangle 8 cm by 3 cm and figure $C$ is a square 5 cm on each side. Compare the areas and choose the best answer.
options: The area of $A$ equals the area of $B$, and the area of $C$ equals the area of $A$.
The area of $A$ equals the area of $B$, and the area of $C$ is greater than the area of $A$.
The area of $A$ is greater than the area of $B$, and the area of $B$ is greater than the area of $C$.
The area of $A$ equals the area of $B$, and the area of $C$ is less than the area of $A$.
blocks.walkthrough: Three numbers first. $A$ is $6 \times 4 = 24$, $B$ is $8 \times 3 = 24$ and $C$ is $5 \times 5 = 25$, all in square centimeters. So $A$ and $B$ match and $C$ beats both by one. Now down the choices: the second is the only one whose two clauses both hold. The last choice is the trap, and it is a trap about the drawing rather than the arithmetic — $C$ is the shortest figure across the page, so it looks like the small one, and it is the biggest by a single square centimeter.

blocks.text: Triangles and composite figures

Two figures cause almost all the arithmetic errors in this question type. The first is the triangle: its area is half the base times the height, and forgetting the half turns a triangle of area 36 into one of area 72, which is enough to reverse the whole ordering. The second is the composite figure, usually an L shape. Cut it into two rectangles, find each area and add them. Treating an L shape as the full rectangle it sits inside inflates the area by the piece that was cut out, and the choices are built to reward exactly that mistake.

blocks.stem: Figure $A$ is a square 6 cm on each side, figure $B$ is a rectangle 9 cm by 4 cm and figure $C$ is a right triangle with legs of 12 cm and 6 cm. Compare the areas and choose the best answer.
options: The area of $A$ is greater than the area of $B$, and the area of $B$ is greater than the area of $C$.
The area of $A$ equals the area of $B$, and the area of $B$ equals the area of $C$.
The area of $A$ equals the area of $B$, and the area of $C$ is greater than the area of $B$.
The area of $A$ equals the area of $B$, and the area of $C$ is less than the area of $B$.
blocks.walkthrough: $A$ is $6 \times 6 = 36$. $B$ is $9 \times 4 = 36$. $C$ is $\frac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 6 = 36$. All three are 36 square centimeters, so the second choice is right and the item is testing one thing only. Skip the half on the triangle and you get 72, which makes $C$ the largest and sends you to the third choice — the choice that is there for precisely that slip. When a figure is a triangle, halve before you compare.

blocks.text: Area and perimeter are independent

This is the fact the question type is built on, and it is worth stating flatly: a figure with a larger area can have a smaller perimeter. A square 6 cm on a side has area 36 and perimeter 24. A rectangle 12 cm by 2 cm has area 24 and perimeter 28. The square has the bigger area and the shorter distance around, and if you rank one measure by looking at the other you will be wrong.

Two more consequences follow. Equal perimeters do not mean equal areas: rectangles 7 cm by 3 cm, 5 cm by 5 cm and 8 cm by 2 cm all have a perimeter of 20 cm and areas of 21, 25 and 16 square centimeters. And equal areas do not mean equal perimeters: a square 6 cm on a side and a rectangle 9 cm by 4 cm both cover 36 square centimeters, but the perimeters are 24 cm and 26 cm. Of all rectangles holding a given area, the square has the shortest perimeter, and the more stretched the rectangle the more edge it needs.

blocks.stem: Figure $A$ is a square 6 cm on each side, figure $B$ is a rectangle 12 cm by 2 cm and figure $C$ is a rectangle 9 cm by 4 cm. Compare the perimeters and choose the best answer.
options: The perimeter of $B$ is less than the perimeter of $C$, and the perimeter of $C$ is less than the perimeter of $A$.
The perimeter of $A$ is less than the perimeter of $C$, and the perimeter of $C$ is less than the perimeter of $B$.
The perimeter of $A$ equals the perimeter of $C$, and the perimeter of $B$ is greater than the perimeter of $A$.
The perimeter of $A$ is greater than the perimeter of $C$, and the perimeter of $C$ is greater than the perimeter of $B$.
blocks.walkthrough: The stem says perimeters, so add the sides and leave the areas alone. $A$ is $4 \times 6 = 24$ cm, $B$ is $2(12) + 2(2) = 28$ cm and $C$ is $2(9) + 2(4) = 26$ cm, giving $A$ less than $C$ less than $B$. Notice what the areas would have told you: 36, 24 and 36 square centimeters. $A$ and $C$ cover the same ground and need different amounts of fence, and $B$ has the smallest area with the longest perimeter. Anyone who ranks this item by area gets a tie at the top and no matching choice.

blocks.text: Angles

Angle items give you two of the angles in each figure and mark the third with an $x$. The only question is what the angles in that figure add to, and there are three answers: a triangle totals $180^\circ$, angles filling a straight line total $180^\circ$, and angles filling the space around a point total $360^\circ$. Subtract the two given angles from the right total and you have $x$. Using $180^\circ$ where the figure needs $360^\circ$ produces negative angles, which is your signal that you picked the wrong total rather than that the item is broken.

head: Where the angles sit
What they add to
rows: The three angles of a triangle
Angles filling the space around a point
The four angles of a quadrilateral
A right angle, marked with a small box
Each angle of an equilateral triangle

blocks.stem: In each of three figures, three rays meet at a point, so the angles around that point add to $360^\circ$. In $A$ the two given angles are $130^\circ$ and $140^\circ$; in $B$ they are $110^\circ$ and $155^\circ$; in $C$ they are $145^\circ$ and $110^\circ$. The third angle in each figure is marked $x$. Choose the best answer.
options: The angle $x$ in $A$ is less than the angle $x$ in $B$, and the angle $x$ in $B$ is less than the angle $x$ in $C$.
The angle $x$ in $C$ is less than the angle $x$ in $B$, and the angle $x$ in $B$ is less than the angle $x$ in $A$.
The angle $x$ in $A$ equals the angle $x$ in $C$, and the angle $x$ in $B$ is less than the angle $x$ in $A$.
The angle $x$ in $A$ equals the angle $x$ in $B$, and the angle $x$ in $C$ is greater than the angle $x$ in $B$.
blocks.walkthrough: Add the two given angles in each figure and subtract from $360$. In $A$, $130 + 140 = 270$ and $360 - 270 = 90$. In $B$, $110 + 155 = 265$ and $360 - 265 = 95$. In $C$, $145 + 110 = 255$ and $360 - 255 = 105$. So $x$ runs $90$, $95$, $105$ and the first choice is right. Subtracting from $180$ instead gives $-90$, $-85$ and $-75$, and because the more negative value belongs to the figure with the largest true angle, that error reverses the ordering and lands you on the second choice.

blocks.text: Comparing lengths

Length items compare labeled segments inside one figure rather than three separate drawings. Three facts carry almost all of them. A square's diagonal is longer than its side, and the two diagonals of a square are equal to each other. In a circle the diameter is the longest chord, so any chord that misses the center is shorter than the diameter, and a chord may be longer or shorter than the radius depending on where it sits. And when a segment is divided at two points, overlapping pieces cancel: comparing $WY$ with $XZ$ on a segment cut at $X$ and $Y$ really comes down to comparing $WX$ with $YZ$, because both totals contain $XY$.

blocks.stem: Square $MNOP$ has sides of 5 cm, and both diagonals, $MO$ and $NP$, have been drawn. Choose the best answer.
options: $MO$ is greater than $MN$, and $MO$ is greater than $NP$.
blocks.walkthrough: $MN$ is a side, so it is 5 cm. $MO$ and $NP$ are the two diagonals of the same square, so they are equal to each other, and a diagonal is always longer than a side — here about 7 cm. Both clauses of the second choice hold. The third choice is the one to watch: its first clause is true, and a student who checks only the clause they were already sure of will take it. In a square the diagonals are always equal, so a choice that makes one longer than the other cannot be right whatever the drawing looks like.

blocks.text: Testing a compound choice

Every choice makes two claims joined by and, and a choice is wrong if either claim is wrong. That is good news, because it means you can often kill a choice by checking one clause. It is also where the points go, since three of the four choices normally contain one true clause and one false one, and a half-true statement reads as correct if you stop after the comma.

items: Cover the second clause and test the first against your three numbers.
If the first clause fails, cross the whole choice out and move on. Do not read the rest of it.
If the first clause holds, uncover the second and test it just as carefully.
Check the clause you are least sure of first when one clause involves a value you computed quickly.

blocks.text: The traps

items: Comparing the wrong measure. The stem names area, perimeter, angle or length. The three figures are built so that the area ordering and the perimeter ordering disagree.
Forgetting to halve a triangle. Area is $\frac{1}{2}bh$. This single slip is the most common wrong answer on area items involving a triangle.
Judging by the drawing. The widest figure is regularly the smallest in area and the tallest triangle regularly has the shortest perimeter. Figures are not drawn to scale.
Assuming equal areas mean equal perimeters, or the reverse. They are independent, and a larger area can come with a smaller perimeter.
Swapping the circle formulas. Area is $\pi r^2$ and the distance around is $2\pi r$. Putting a radius into $\pi d$ halves the circumference and puts the circle last in the ranking.
Treating a composite figure as the rectangle around it. Split an L shape into two rectangles and add. The uncut rectangle is always an available wrong answer.
Using the wrong angle total. Angles around a point make $360^\circ$, not $180^\circ$. If your angle comes out negative, you used the wrong total.
Accepting a half-true choice. Both clauses have to hold. Test them one at a time.

blocks.text: When you are stuck

items: Compute the value you are surest of and eliminate on it alone. If you know $A$ is 24, every choice that makes $A$ the largest is gone, and that usually removes two.
Look for the equals sign. These items are written so that two of the three figures very often come out the same, so check the choices containing $=$ first.
Rank instead of calculating exactly. A circle of radius 3 cm has area a bit over 28 square centimeters, which is enough to place it between 27 and 36 without touching $\pi$ again.
Guess and move on. There is no penalty for a wrong answer on the HSPT, and one geometry item is not worth the three series questions it would cost you.

blocks.text: Worth memorizing

items: The six area formulas in the table above, and that a triangle takes the half.
Circle: area $\pi r^2$, distance around $2\pi r$, diameter $2r$, $\pi \approx 3.14$.
The angle totals: $180^\circ$ for a triangle and for a straight line, $360^\circ$ around a point and for a quadrilateral.
A square's diagonal is longer than its side, and the two diagonals of a square are equal.
The diameter is the longest chord in a circle.
Area and perimeter are independent. The bigger figure is not automatically the one with more edge.
